az_2_bear_canyon.blurb: Bear Canyon sits along the Catalina Highway on Mount Lemmon in the Santa Catalina Mountains above Tucson, at roughly 5,000 feet. The setting is shady, among ponderosa pine, and lower on the mountain than you might expect. Trad is the largest share of the climbing, with sport close behind, plus a solid collection of boulder problems and a few top-ropes. Roped grades run from easy fifth class up to 5.13, but most climbs land between 5.9 and 5.11. Boulder problems go from very easy to about V7. Chimney Rock is known for long classic trad pitches, the Chessman Area is mostly bolted, and Peanut Boulders hold the biggest cluster of problems. Across the whole highway the crags span many elevations and aspects, so the mountain can be climbed year-round.

or_central_oregon_bouldering.blurb: Nearly all of the climbing here is bouldering, scattered across many small zones around Bend, with a smaller cluster near Sisters. Many zones follow the Deschutes River, Tumalo Creek or forest roads. The Depot is a basalt cliff band above the river, Meadow Camp is a long welded tuff cliff line in the forest, Widgi Creek hides about thirty boulders among the trees, and Mile Marker 5 has shaded boulders with flat landings. Grades start at V0 and most problems fall between V1 and V5, with a thin tail of hard ones up to V11. Expect everything from low traverses to tall highballs, short walks of 5 to 25 minutes, and quiet corners. Shade and river air make some spots workable on hot days.

sd_rapid_city_area.blurb: Around Rapid City, on the edge of the Black Hills, the climbing splits into limestone and sandstone. Hard sport routes on limestone at The VC, Bethlehem and the Dalton Lake area are the draw for strong climbers, with most sport grades between 5.10 and 5.13. Falling Rock is a small limestone canyon close to town, mostly bolted and top-roped; its south-facing wall stays warm enough for winter days while the north wall suits warm ones. Bouldering is on sandstone, with Rock Maze the best known: problems from V0 to V9 over good landings, with Bone Collector and Bogus Jim also popular. Summers are hot and dry, winters cold but fairly mild, and picking the right crag keeps you climbing most of the year.

id_castle_rocks.blurb: Castle Rocks lies in the high desert of south-central Idaho, next to its better-known granite neighbor. Climbs go up granite spires and monoliths ringed by desert scrub. Trad has a slight edge over sport, with a good number of boulder problems too. Grades run from moderate to 5.13, and most routes are 5.8 to 5.11. The routes were put up more recently than those next door, so protection tends to be modern, with closer bolt spacing and good hardware. Some descents need more than one rope. Lower elevation makes it a decent choice on cold days; spring and fall are the best times, summers are hot and winters snowy. It sees far fewer climbers than its neighbor, and approaches run longer.

ar_river_valley_and_ouachitas_region.blurb: This region covers the climbing south of the Arkansas River, mostly sandstone whose texture turns harder and more quartzite-like toward the south. Sport leads, with a fair amount of bouldering and a thin trad scene. Roped grades stretch from easy to 5.13, and most fall in the 5.9 to 5.12 range; boulder problems run from V0 to V10. Mount Magazine, the state's highest point, is one of the oldest destinations, with bluffs of harder, less friction-friendly rock and south-facing walls that catch winter sun. Dardanelle Rock is mostly sport at 5.10 and up. Petit Jean is newer, with Hartshorne Sandstone bluffs set in an intimate hollow landscape. The Whitcombs and Woods Mountain are bouldering spots.
